summary.summary: Camden took no new borrowing in 2025/26 and held external debt flat at £294m (£169m PWLB at 4.57%, £124m LOBOs at 4.43%, £1m community bond), but its CFR jumped £50m to £812m, pushing under-borrowing (capital spend financed from its own cash instead of loans) to £518m. The council says this internal borrowing saves about £10.4m a year versus borrowing at current rates, but also that planned use of earmarked reserves will create an external borrowing requirement within 12-24 months, and that investments were drawn down in-year to support cash flow as service demand outpaced funding. Headline investments of £197m flatter the picture: £159m of that is held on behalf of the North London Waste Authority. The report itself flags a greater likelihood that LOBO lenders will exercise their rate-reset options as market rates have risen. A £6.4m loan was made in April 2025 to wholly-owned Camden Living Housing Association; all prudential indicators were met.

signals.headline: £124m of LOBO loans (average rate 4.43%, average life ~25 years); council states higher market rates make lender rate-reset calls more likely, with repayment at par the fallback
signals.why: A called LOBO would force Camden to refinance or repay a slice of £124m at today's much higher rates, exactly when its cash buffer is being run down.

signals.headline: Investments drawn down in 2025/26 to support cash flow and service delivery; planned earmarked-reserve usage expected to create an external borrowing requirement within 12-24 months on top of £518m under-borrowing
signals.why: The cheap internal-borrowing strategy ends when the reserves funding it are spent, converting a deferred liability into real borrowing at ~6% PWLB rates.

signals.headline: £6.4m loan advanced 24 April 2025 to wholly-owned Camden Living Housing Association to buy 34 social-rent homes, with about 10 more purchases planned
signals.why: Council cash is now exposed to a housing subsidiary's ability to service debt from social rents.

compliance.notes: A strong, well-evidenced inner-London TMSS. Strongest on the prudential/treasury indicators and MRP: capital plans, CFR, gross-debt-vs-CFR and financing-cost ratios are all multi-year (2024/25 actual to 2028/29), split GF/HRA and reconciled; the liability benchmark is charted to 2064/65; the investment/creditworthiness strategy prioritises security-liquidity-yield and drives rating-based counterparty limits and durations using CDS/market data beyond ratings; and the MRP policy is comprehensive, asset-life-justified and full-council approved. Weakest area is the commercial/non-treasury investment framework: no paragraphs 51-53 compliance statement (COM-02), no proportionality-to-financial-capacity demonstration (core COM-03 only partial), and no separate purpose-based reporting, IMPs, security/income-dependence disclosures, exit review or clear nil statement (COM-04/05/07/08/11 absent). Other notable gaps: no formal adoption of the CIPFA TM Code's four clauses (core GOV-01, only 'have regard to'); no explicit fixed/variable interest-rate exposure limits (core RISK-02); no separate HRA/GF liability benchmark despite material HRA debt (LB-04); and minor omissions on sterling-only borrowing (BOR-03), audit-qualification flagging (RPT-05), derivatives policy (RISK-06) and segregation of duties (GOV-08). Scored from the Cabinet 25 Feb / Full Council 2 March 2026 report (CS/2026/08) and its Appendix 1 TMSS 2026/27; no separate capital strategy was read.

news_drafts.headline: Camden repays £29m LOBO loan after lender proposed 7.77%, replacing it with PWLB borrowing at 4.69%
news_drafts.lead:
Camden Council repaid a £29m bank loan on 27 August 2026 after the lender, FMS Wertmanagement, proposed raising its interest rate from 4.625% to 7.77%. The loan was a LOBO loan (a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher rate and the council may then repay in full instead of accepting it). The council's Audit and Corporate Governance Committee, meeting on 24 September, received the details in a treasury management update (a report on how the council borrows and manages its cash).

FMS notified the council of the proposed rise on 20 August. The council used its right to repay rather than accept. On 2 September it took out a replacement £29m loan for two years from the PWLB (Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils) at 4.69%, a rate that includes a discount for its housing revenue account (the ring-fenced account for council homes). The paper puts the new loan's interest at about £1.360m a year, which it says avoids about £893,000 a year compared with the FMS rate. It costs about £19,000 a year more than the original loan did.

The paper lists three more FMS loans with lender option dates: £15m on 24 September, £25m on 9 October and £10m on 29 October, £50m in all. It says further borrowing or refinancing (replacing old loans with new ones) may be needed during 2026/27, depending on "lender decisions, cash flow requirements, capital financing obligations, and prevailing interest rates".

findings.paper_title: Homes & Communities Performance Report - Quarter 1 2026/27 (April to June 2026)
findings.headline: Housing register grew to 9,144 households in Q1 from 8,984 in Q4
findings.detail: The housing register added 160 households to reach 9,144 in Q1. Only 178 social housing lets were made in the quarter. The paper attributes growth to 'ongoing pressure on housing supply and affordability across the borough'.
findings.matters: A large and growing register indicates persistent unmet demand and future service cost pressure on lettings and housing solutions services.
findings.figures: Households on housing register: 8544 (Q2) → 8751 (Q3) → 8984 (Q4) → 9144 (Q1); social housing lets: 157 (Q2) → 249 (Q3) → 217 (Q4) → 178 (Q1)
findings.quote: Number of households on the housing register 8544 8751 8984 9144

findings.paper_title: Homes & Communities Performance Report - Quarter 1 2026/27 (April to June 2026)
findings.headline: Households in temporary accommodation increased to 1,428 in Q1, with 724 involving children
findings.detail: The number of households in temporary accommodation rose from 1,393 in Q4 to 1,428 in Q1, a 35-household increase. Those with children grew to 724 (50.7% of the total). The paper states that 'demand continues to outstrip the availability of permanent housing' despite a slight reduction in newly placed households (121 vs 123).
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a high-cost service; its continuing upward trajectory despite homelessness prevention efforts indicates structural supply pressure requiring sustained investment.
findings.figures: Households in temporary accommodation: 1188 (Q2) → 1372 (Q3) → 1393 (Q4) → 1428 (Q1); with children: 567 → 676 → 690 → 724; newly placed: 157 → 162 → 123 → 121
findings.quote: Number of households living in temporary accommodation 1188 1372 1393 1428

findings.paper_title: Homes & Communities Performance Report - Quarter 1 2026/27 (April to June 2026)
findings.headline: Non-emergency responsive repairs completion rate fell to 73.8% from 82.4% in the prior quarter
findings.detail: Performance on non-emergency repairs declined significantly from 82.4% in Q4 to 73.8% in Q1, reversing a trajectory of improvement. Emergency repairs remained closer to target at 86.0%. Overdue repairs rose slightly from 1,372 to 1,434. The paper does not specify the cause of the deterioration.
findings.matters: Declining repairs performance may indicate operational or resource constraints that could affect resident satisfaction and future remedial costs.
findings.figures: Proportion of non-emergency responsive repairs completed within target: 89% (Q2) → 88% (Q3) → 82.4% (Q4) → 73.8% (Q1); Overdue repairs awaiting completion: 2436 (Q2) → 2165 (Q3) → 1372 (Q4) → 1434 (Q1)
findings.quote: Proportion of non-emergency responsive repairs completed within the landlord's target timescale [LCRA only] (%) 89% 88% 82.4% 73.8%

findings.paper_title: Homes & Communities Performance Report - Quarter 1 2026/27 (April to June 2026)
findings.headline: Tenancy evictions due to rent arrears increased to 10 in Q1 from 2 in Q4
findings.detail: The number of evictions for rent arrears jumped from 2 in Q4 to 10 in Q1, a five-fold increase. This occurs alongside overall improvement in rent collection and reduction in accounts with high arrears, suggesting some tenancies face acute financial distress despite aggregate improvement.
findings.matters: Rising evictions signal emerging tenancy distress and potential cost from homelessness prevention and support services.
findings.figures: Number of tenancy evictions due to rent arrears: 5 (Q2) → 4 (Q3) → 2 (Q4) → 10 (Q1)
findings.quote: Number of tenancy evictions due to rent arrears 5 4 2 10

findings.paper_title: Homes & Communities Performance Report - Quarter 1 2026/27 (April to June 2026)
findings.headline: Rent collection exceeded amount due at 101.2% in Q1, with rent accounts in significant arrears down to 207
findings.detail: Council tenants paid rent equivalent to 101.2% of the amount due in Q1, continuing an improvement trajectory from 100.7% two years prior. The number of rent accounts with arrears above £10,000 fell to 207 from 303 a year earlier, and rent arrears as a percentage of the rent roll fell to 6.1% from 8.3%.
findings.matters: Rent collection above 100% is uncommon and signals strong income management; this is material to a lender given the council manages high demand for housing services and temporary accommodation.
findings.figures: Rent collected as % of rent due: 100.7% (Q2) → 100.4% (Q3) → 101.1% (Q4) → 101.2% (Q1); Rent accounts with arrears above £10,000: 303 (Q2) → 284 (Q3) → 259 (Q4) → 207 (Q1); Rent arrears as % of rent roll: 8.3% (Q2) → 8.2% (Q3) → 7.5% (Q4) → 6.1% (Q1)
findings.quote: Rent collected as a % of rent due for all council tenants 100.7% 100.4% 101.1% 101.2%
